item.title: A Raspberry Pi MS-DOS Build
item.description:
Introduction

As a ‘young’ Millennial, I grew up in the late 90s and early 2000s. Even then, for a variety of reasons, my family often lagged a generation behind on tech. As such, I grew up on late MS-DOS games alongside early Windows games, and due to nostalgia and my growing interest in the fundamental ways computers work, I’ve developed a greater interest in retro computers and games.

Over the early months of 2026, I also found myself developing an interest in single-board computers (Raspberry Pi) and microcontrollers, but I needed a basic project that I could start off with, so I decided to give this a try. I really want to get into retro computing proper, but it’s not a cheap hobby by any means. Instead, I decided to combine these two recent interests as a starter Pi project and build a “nostalgia box” to relive some level of my early childhood experiences on PC!

item.title: An Unnecessarily Complicated Framework: my blog pipeline
item.description:
If you’re reading this blog, chances are that you don’t realize how complicated things are behind the scenes. What looks like a visually-appealing, easy-to-view blog for my career, home lab and tech opinions is actually several Git(hub) repositories publishing markdown files piped in direct from my primary Obsidian vault.

Why did I do it this way, when spinning up something like a WordPress blog would’ve been so much simpler and easier?

item.title: Network Nightmare [Troubleshooting Tales #1]
item.description: In over eight months of using Manjaro Linux as my daily driver, I’ve encountered a handful of oddities and issues that I’ve had to sink a few hours into fixing. By and large, the experience has been smooth, but when something breaks, it seems to break randomly and without immediately apparent cause. I just dealt with another such situation and figured I would write down what I did to fix the issue as part of a new post series I’m starting: “Troubleshooting Tales”.

item.title: Pixel Locked - Staying Secure as a PC Gamer
item.description: Are you a PC gamer? Do you take appropriate measures to keep your game accounts safe? Chances are, unless you’re a security nerd like myself, you might not be threat modeling with your gaming accounts. It’s extremely important, especially as your accounts’ libraries grow and you interact more with the different platforms’ communities (if they have one), which gradually raises the real-world value of your accounts. In this post, I will offer some tips that any user can implement to better protect your valuable PC gaming libraries!

item.title: A Key-nundrum - Staying secure with asymmetric encryption
item.description:
Asymmetric encryption, also known as public key cryptography, is a common form of encryption utilized today. It’s used constantly during web traffic, specifically during the TLS handshake. It’s also used in end-to-end encrypted messengers (WhatsApp, Signal, etc.) and with Web3/cryptocurrency wallets, among other things. More recently, it has been utilized to develop passkeys, often lauded as the next generation of online security.

Whether you’re a geek or not, you’re using it on a daily basis for one thing or another, even if you don’t necessarily realize it.

item.title: On Discouragement - Lessons from Career Failures
item.description:
I’ve had no shortage of disappointments in my adult life. In fact, I’ve tried three separate careers before now, and every one of them has failed miserably. I’m on my fourth career attempt and have run into the same sorts of road blocks I ran into with my previous career attempts, so what keeps me going? It’s not as cut-and-dry as one might suspect, which surprises even me.

Some Background

In high school, I was passionate and determined to become a game developer. In almost all of my spare time back then, I’d do a combination of making games and modding existing games. I was working on an open world 2D adventure game with an art style that (unintentionally) resembled a more colorful Ultima 5, but with intentions to mirror the free, open exploration of my favorite game series, The Elder Scrolls. I also did experiment with other games, including a marble maze game made in GameMaker (specifically 8.1, in the days before they moved to the GameMaker Studio branch). I had every intention to work for one of my then-favorite studios, from Jagex in the United Kingdom, to Bethesda in Maryland… but eventually, I decided I wanted to start my own studio instead.

item.title: Frustrations, Humblings and Revelations - A Second Beginning on Linux
item.description: Back in August on my old blog, I ran through my thought processes on picking a Linux distribution to use on my primary PC. By the end of that lengthy blog post, I had talked about how I was leaning toward Manjaro, with Fedora as a possible secondary option. Much of my reasoning for leaning toward Manjaro had to do with a blend of features, a middle ground on the rolling release through the Manjaro Stable branch and so forth. Well, I did decide to go for Manjaro as my primary workstation distro after all and, well… what ensued was a series of frustration after frustration that led me to some degree of discouragement and humbling. Let’s talk about it.

item.title: Learning Ubuntu Server 1 - Beginnings
item.description:
I’ve gradually purchased more and more courses on Packt for side projects, such as learning Linux or machine learning. Back in August, I worked on one that taught me how to install, configure and use Arch Linux, which was the last major wall that I was facing when it comes to my learning of the basics of the various major Linux distribution types.

Now, I’m moving on to something a bit more practical: Ubuntu Server Mastery - Real-World Linux Admin Skills by the same course author, Dan Mill. In this blog post series, “Learning Ubuntu Server”, I will be documenting my progress through this course to show what I’ve learned and what I’ve reinforced.

item.title: Navigating Linux Distros - My Personal Journey
item.description: I, like many others, made the decision to switch to Linux for my primary PC following the death of Windows 10. I already take a lot of issues with modern Windows as it is, and decided I wasn’t willing to use the privacy nightmare that is Windows 11 (excluding one of my side systems, which I’ll talk about in future posts). Plus, with my ongoing career change into IT and cybersecurity, I knew Linux was going to be a necessity so I have about three years of experience experimenting with it at this point.
